subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: doing everything alone out of duty [Pitfall]
passage: Parul believed that caring for her parents was her job alone. Her brother Irfan lived overseas, and she never asked him for anything. There was no spare money for help, either. Every evening after work she cooked, sorted the tablets, took her father to the clinic, and slept in a chair by her mother's bed. By spring she was making mistakes on the accounts, a wrong total on the Monday report and then another, and her supervisor spoke to her quietly. At home she snapped at her mother over a spilled cup and saw her mother flinch. That night Parul sat in the dark kitchen, too tired to eat, and thought: this is not caring, this is only surviving. She did not yet know who to call. But she knew she had to.

qa.q: Where did Parul's brother Irfan live?
What was Parul feeling when her mother flinched?
qa.a: Parul felt guilty and worn out, realising she had hurt the person she was trying to look after.

qa.q: What other approach could Parul try?
qa.a: She could tell Irfan and other relatives exactly which tasks need doing and ask each to take a share, and look into paid help, because sharing the load protects both her and her parents.

qa.q: How might Parul's mother have experienced those months?
qa.a: Parul's mother may have felt hurt and guilty about being a burden, and confused by the sharp words.

grounding: Parul takes on all her parents' care alone after work and ends up exhausted, making errors and short-tempered.

subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: doing everything alone out of duty [Pitfall]
passage:
Every evening at six-thirty, Pooja left her Pune office and went straight to her parents' flat. Cooking, medicines, her father's dressing, her mother's blood-pressure reading, dishes. Home by eleven.
"You should get help," her colleague Kalyani said one day.
"They're my parents. It's my job."
Her brother lived in Bengaluru and sent money. Pooja never asked for more. Asking felt like failing.
By the third month, she was falling asleep on the bus. At work she sent a client the wrong invoice and missed a deadline. Her manager called her in.
One evening, her mother asked for her tea to be less sweet. Pooja snapped, "Can't you just drink it?" Her mother went quiet. Her father looked away.
On the bus home, Pooja stared at her reflection in the window. She had been trying so hard to be a good daughter, and she had just made her mother feel like a burden.

qa.q: What time did Pooja leave her office each evening?
How did Pooja feel on the bus home after snapping at her mother?
qa.a: Pooja felt guilty and exhausted, ashamed that her effort to be a good daughter had made her mother feel like a burden.

qa.q: What else could Pooja have done instead of managing everything alone?
qa.a: She could have asked her brother to share tasks or pay for some daytime help, and looked at a schedule that included rest for herself.

qa.q: How is Pooja's mother affected by Pooja doing everything alone?
qa.a: Her mother goes quiet and likely feels hurt and like a burden when Pooja, worn out, snaps at her over tea.

grounding: It shows a daughter who believes all care is her duty managing it alone after work, becoming exhausted, making work errors and snapping at her parents.

subtopic: Caring for ageing parents while working
subtype: Approach: doing everything alone out of duty [Pitfall]
passage:
"Rehana, you look terrible. When did you last sleep properly?"
"Ayesha, don't start."
"I'm serious. You're at your parents' every evening and every weekend."
"Who else will do it? Abbu can't manage his insulin alone, and Ammi's knees are bad. I'm their daughter."
"You have two brothers."
"They're busy."
"So are you. You told me you nearly sent the wrong file to the audit team yesterday."
Rehana rubbed her eyes. "It's just a bad week."
"It's been a bad four months. And yesterday you shouted at your mother because she asked for salt."
Rehana was quiet. "I felt awful after. She just looked at me."
"You're not failing by asking for help. You're failing by pretending you don't need it."
Rehana stared into her cold tea. "I don't even know how to ask them."
"Start with one day a week. Call your brothers tonight."

qa.q: What did Rehana nearly do at work yesterday?
qa.a: She nearly sent the wrong file to the audit team.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel after shouting at her mother?
qa.a: Rehana felt awful and guilty, remembering how her mother just looked at her.

qa.q: What small step could help Rehana most right now?
qa.a: She could call her brothers tonight and ask each to take one day a week, so she gets some rest.

qa.q: How does Rehana's situation look to Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha sees her friend exhausted and making mistakes, and is worried enough to push Rehana to ask for help.

grounding: It shows a daughter who sees care as her duty doing it all alone after work until she is exhausted, makes work errors and snaps at her parents.
